newsitem.title: USA: Record money goes to U.S. Congress election battle.
newsitem.headline: Record money goes to U.S. Congress election battle.

text.p: Record sums of money are being raised by Democrats and Republicans in their battle to control the U.S. Congress, with analysts estimating the total may approach $1 billion by the Nov. 5 election.

The independent Centre for Responsive Politics estimated last week that direct campaign contributions alone would reach more than $800 million as Democrats fight to regain control from the Republicans and analysts say indirect contributions will boost the total far higher.

Federal Election Commission and party officials said at least $110 million in campaign contributions had gone into 18 Senate races that are up for grabs and will decide who controls the 100-member body next year.
Over $97 million had gone to 100 key races that will decide control of the 435-member House of Representatives.

Campaign analysts give Democrats only an outside chance of winning back the Senate but they say the Democrats' prospect of winning the House is even. Republicans won both chambers in the 1994 elections for the first time in 40 years.
The election commission's latest total, which includes only contributions in the 18 months to the end of June, stood at $448 million amassed in candidates' coffers.

But national party campaign committees have pumped tens of millions more into the races and nearly half of campaign money usually comes in the final months of the campaigns, leading analysts to expect a final figure of close to $1 billion.
The FEC said contributions by the end of June 1994, were $388 million but the total reached $740 million.

Indirect money yet to come includes most of a controversial $35 million war chest that labour unions have targeted against vulnerable Republicans to help Democrats win the 18 seats they need to take back control of the House.
The 14-million member American Federation of Labour and Congress of Industrial Organisations (AFL-CIO) is trying to help with television ads against 30 of the most vulnerable Republican freshmen.

In each case the ads play on the unpopularity of House Speaker Newt Gingrich, accusing the Republicans of voting with Gingrich "to cut Medicare and give new tax breaks to the wealthy" or "to cut college loans."

The National Republican Congressional Committee countered with a television ad in each of the 30 campaigns saying: "The big labour bosses in Washington are spending big money spreading big lies to buy their control of Congress."
Outraged Republicans have filed lawsuits accusing the AFL-CIO of illegally trying the buy the House with the money.

But the labour organisation says those are "voter education" ads, not campaign ads subject to federal campaign laws. It said corporations and national Republican committees spend even more money for such ads.
Corporation and trade group political committees contributed $85 million to congressional campaigns as of June 30, and labour committees contributed $26 million.

The Centre for Responsive Politics reported that the biggest such contributors to presidential and congressional campaigns were tobacco company Philip Morris, communications firm AT&T, a trial lawyers' group and the Teamsters Union.
It is in races for the Senate, where the Democrats need to make a net gain of four seats, that the big money has gone.

More than $15 million has been pumped into the fight for a North Carolina seat in which Democrat Harvey Gantt was trying for the second time to beat conservative Senator Jesse Helms. Of that, $11.5 million has gone to Helms.
Another $11.2 million has gone into the battle in New Jersey between Republican Representative Dick Zimmer and Democratic Representative Robert Torricelli to replace retiring Senator Bill Bradley.

Senator Larry Pressler of South Dakota, one of the most vulnerable Republicans, has received $3.7 million in contributions. One of the most vulnerable Democrats, Senator Paul Wellstone of Minnesota, has received $5.3 million.
